historical_timeline.summary: Campaigns against the English in James Bay and Hudson Bay, with scurvy among the men.
Chose the site of Fort Maurepas on Biloxi Bay, beginning the Louisiana colony.
Forced by illness to put in at Pensacola on his third voyage.
Recurrent attacks of an illness his biographer calls malaria; did not return to Louisiana.
Entrusted with preparing an armament for the West Indies.
Martinique and the capture of Nevis.

claims.statement: Pierre Le Moyne d'Iberville was born on July 16, 1661, in Montreal (Ville-Marie), New France, and was baptized there on July 20, 1661. He was the third son of Charles Le Moyne de Longueuil et de Châteauguay and Catherine Thierry.
claims.clinical_interpretation: The Dictionary of Canadian Biography and the Canadian Encyclopedia give only the baptism; 64 Parishes gives the birth date.

claims.statement: The name d'Iberville came from a fief held by his father's family near Dieppe, and d'Ardillières from a property he acquired in Aunis near Rochefort. He was the first person born in Canada to receive the cross of the order of Saint-Louis.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Explains the territorial designations in his name.

claims.statement: He fought the English in Hudson Bay and James Bay from 1686: the capture of the James Bay posts in 1686, the Albany River in 1688 to 1689, New Severn in 1690, York Fort (renamed Fort Bourbon) in 1694, and in 1697 the naval battle near York Factory in which his ship, the Pélican, defeated English warships and was itself lost, followed by the surrender of the fort.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Career context: years of winter campaigning in the subarctic.

claims.statement: His biographer records that scurvy and exposure killed 25 of the English in the winter of 1688 to 1689 on the Albany River, and that in 1694 at York Fort scurvy killed many men on both sides.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Documents scurvy among the men of these campaigns, not in Iberville himself; the roster's 'scurvy' is not supported as his own illness.

claims.statement: In 1696 to 1697 he led a campaign against the English: Fort William Henry at Pemaquid capitulated on August 15, 1696, and in Newfoundland St John's surrendered on November 30 after a brief siege; the campaign destroyed 36 settlements, killed about 200 people and took about 700 prisoners.

He led the expeditions that began the French colony of Louisiana: in April 1699 he chose a site near the entrance of Biloxi Bay, near present-day Ocean Springs, Mississippi, for Fort Maurepas; in 1700 he built a fort on the Mississippi; and on his third voyage he began Fort Saint-Louis at Mobile. He left Louisiana in April 1702 and did not return.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Career context; anchors his service on the Gulf Coast.

source_links.locator: Fort Maurepas, Fort Mississipi, Mobile, April 1702

claims.statement: Sailing from La Rochelle on September 29, 1701, on his third voyage to Louisiana, he was forced by illness to put in at Pensacola.
claims.clinical_interpretation: The nature of the illness is not recorded. No source fetched mentions an abscess.

claims.statement: His biographer writes that he had attacks of malaria that recurred several times from 1702 to 1705 and that his deteriorating health thwarted planned expeditions to Louisiana; 64 Parishes writes that illness kept him from the expedition of 1703.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Documented recurrent illness in the years before the synthetic episode. 'Malaria' is the biographer's word; no contemporary diagnosis or species is known. Anchors the modern relapsing malaria, which is synthetic.

source_links.locator: missed the 1703 expedition due to illness

claims.statement: Despite his poor health, he was well enough in 1705 to be entrusted with preparing an armament, and early in 1706 he sailed from France with a squadron of twelve vessels against the English in the West Indies.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Places him in France preparing a tropical campaign during the synthetic episode.

claims.statement: His biographer places the births of three of his children at La Rochelle, in 1698, 1701 and 1705.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Used only to place his household at La Rochelle; no fact about the children is used.

claims.statement: In the spring of 1706 his squadron reached Martinique and then took the English island of Nevis, whose entire population was taken prisoner, including about 6,000 enslaved Africans, who were seized with the ships, plantations and buildings.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Documented history, stated plainly. No health fact about any of the people seized is recorded.

claims.statement: He died suddenly, probably at Havana, Cuba, probably on July 9, 1706, of an illness his biographer calls unspecified, and was buried the same day in the church of San Cristóbal; 64 Parishes says the site of his burial is unknown.

source_links.locator: died July 9, 1706, in Havana; burial site unknown

claims.statement: The Canadian Encyclopedia says he died likely of yellow fever, and 64 Parishes says he died of yellow fever.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Retrospective attribution; the Dictionary of Canadian Biography calls the illness unspecified. No source fetched names typhus. Not used in the modern episode, which makes no prediction.

synthetic_episode.teaching_objective: Primary care and travel medicine for a 43-year-old naval commander with recurrent fevers after service in malaria-endemic areas, who is preparing to lead a deployment to French Guiana and the French Antilles: recognizing relapsing Plasmodium vivax malaria after blood-stage treatment without antirelapse therapy, using PCR when smears are negative between attacks, testing G6PD quantitatively before primaquine, radical cure with chloroquine and primaquine, and relapse surveillance; then a full pre-travel consultation under the CDC Yellow Book 1705 and the IDSA travel medicine guideline: one dose of yellow fever vaccine and a valid certificate for French Guiana, hepatitis A, hepatitis B and typhoid vaccines, atovaquone-proguanil chemoprophylaxis, mosquito avoidance for dengue and chikungunya (no dengue vaccine for travelers), repellents for typhus, food and water precautions with standby treatment for travelers' diarrhea, terminal antirelapse therapy and fever evaluation after return; preventive care at 43; and a same-day visit for a skin abscess managed by drainage alone under the IDSA skin and soft tissue guideline.

documentation.chief_complaint: Two-week follow-up of recurrent fevers, seen the same day in infectious diseases

hpi.narrative: Mr. Le Moyne d'Iberville returns two weeks after his first visit, on the day of his infectious diseases consultation with Dr. Okonkwo-Hale. He has had no fever, chills or sweats since then. The intake blood smears and rapid antigen test were negative, and the PCR sent to the reference laboratory at intake has detected Plasmodium vivax DNA. His quantitative G6PD activity is normal. He is not on any medicine and has no allergies. He is keen to be treated before the squadron's preparations take up all his time.

Sclerae white; mild conjunctival pallor

assessment_plan.assessment: The presenting fevers now have their explanation. Three attacks of fever with chills, each months after leaving an area where P. vivax predominates, after blood-stage treatment alone, and P. vivax DNA in blood between attacks, fit relapses from dormant liver stages. Hemoglobin 13.0 g/dL and platelets 141 x10^3/uL are slightly low, consistent with recent attacks. G6PD activity 11.8 U/g Hb is normal, so primaquine is safe. Dr. Okonkwo-Hale recommends chloroquine for the blood stage, because P. vivax from the Central American coast is chloroquine-sensitive, with primaquine for radical cure

documentation.chief_complaint: Pre-travel visit for a naval deployment to French Guiana and the French Antilles

hpi.narrative: Mr. Le Moyne d'Iberville, now 44, returns for his pre-travel vaccines. The squadron is expected to sail early next year for the French Antilles and French Guiana, with weeks ashore near Cayenne and Kourou and possible river work inland, and he expects to be away for many months. He has had no fever since his malaria treatment four months ago. The PCR drawn at his last malaria review was negative. The forearm abscess healed within ten days; the culture grew methicillin-susceptible Staphylococcus aureus, and he needed no antibiotic. His screening tests from the preventive visit were negative for HIV and hepatitis C, and the hepatitis B panel shows he is not immune and has never been infected. He has no egg or gelatin allergy, no thymus disease, no immune-suppressing illness or treatment, and has never had yellow fever vaccine.

He has had no fever since his malaria treatment seven months ago. He will be aboard ship for the crossing and in the islands, then ashore near Cayenne and Kourou, possibly with river work inland where malaria is transmitted. He will be responsible for the health measures of his crews and wants to set the example. He asked what he should carry.

referral.question: Three episodes of fever with shaking chills and sweats in two years, each beginning months after naval service in malaria-endemic areas, the first called malaria abroad and treated with chloroquine alone, in a 43-year-old naval commander who is afebrile today. Please establish whether these are malaria relapses, advise on antirelapse treatment, and plan his pre-travel care for a deployment to French Guiana and the French Antilles expected early next year
referral.urgency: Within two weeks; same day if he develops a fever
referral.pertinent_history: Three febrile attacks in two years, each lasting about a week with chills every other day, drenching sweats and headache; the first diagnosed abroad as malaria on a smear, species not recorded, and treated with chloroquine alone; the later two treated with chloroquine without testing; the last ended six weeks ago. Earlier service on the Caribbean coast of Central America and in the Gulf of Mexico. No other illness, no regular medicines, no allergies. Afebrile today; temperature 36.7 C, blood pressure 124/78, pulse 70; spleen not palpable. Thick and thin smears and the rapid antigen test today are negative; Plasmodium species PCR sent to the reference laboratory. Hemoglobin 13.0 g/dL, platelets 141 x10^3/uL, white cells 5.6 x10^3/uL, bilirubin 1.1 mg/dL, ALT 34 U/L, AST 29 U/L, creatinine 0.98 mg/dL (eGFR 98), glucose 92 mg/dL. consultant_note.history: Mr. Le Moyne d'Iberville, a 43-year-old naval commander, is seen at the request of Dr. Delacroix-Boateng for recurrent fevers. Over two years he has had three attacks, each about a week of fever with shaking chills every other day, drenching sweats and headache, each beginning months after he left a posting on the Caribbean coast of Central America or the Gulf of Mexico. The first attack was diagnosed as malaria on a smear abroad, species not recorded, and all three were treated with chloroquine alone; he has never taken primaquine or tafenoquine. The last attack ended eight weeks ago and he has had no fever since. He takes no medicines and has no allergies. He is preparing a squadron for a deployment to the French Antilles and French Guiana early next year, with months ashore and possible inland river work
consultant_note.data_reviewed: Dr. Delacroix-Boateng's intake note and tests: thick and thin smears and rapid antigen test negative; Plasmodium species PCR from the intake sample, reported this week, detected P. vivax DNA; hemoglobin 13.0 g/dL, platelets 141 x10^3/uL, white cells 5.6 x10^3/uL, bilirubin 1.1 mg/dL, ALT 34 U/L, AST 29 U/L, creatinine 0.98 mg/dL, glucose 92 mg/dL; quantitative G6PD activity 11.8 U/g Hb, within the laboratory's normal range

Spleen tip not palpable; liver not enlarged

assessment.assessment: Attacks months after leaving areas where P. vivax predominates, after blood-stage treatment alone, with P. vivax DNA detected between attacks, are relapses from dormant liver stages (hypnozoites). The PCR detects parasites below the threshold of the smear. Mildly low hemoglobin and platelets fit recent attacks. No further diagnostic test is needed. Central American P. vivax is chloroquine-sensitive. With a normal quantitative G6PD, primaquine 30 mg base daily for 14 days is appropriate; at 68 kg that dose meets the total recommended dose

assessment.display: Pre-travel care for French Guiana and the French Antilles
assessment.assessment: French Guiana requires proof of yellow fever vaccination from all arriving travelers, and CDC recommends it; one dose gives long-lasting protection. Hepatitis A, hepatitis B (if not immune) and typhoid vaccines are recommended for a long stay. Malaria is transmitted in parts of French Guiana, mostly P. vivax with some P. falciparum and chloroquine resistance, so chloroquine is not suitable for prophylaxis there. Dengue, chikungunya and rickettsial infections including typhus are prevented by vector avoidance; no dengue vaccine is recommended for travelers

recommendations: Chloroquine 1,000 mg salt now, then 500 mg at 6, 24 and 48 hours, for the blood stage
Primaquine 30 mg base daily with food for 14 days for radical cure, starting today; stop and seek care for dark urine, breathlessness or blue lips
Blood smear and PCR about a week after the last primaquine dose, with a blood count and bilirubin; then no routine tests, but a smear the same day for any fever

Pre-travel vaccines at least a month before departure: yellow fever with the international certificate, hepatitis A, typhoid Vi, and hepatitis B if the screening panel shows he is not immune; influenza in the autumn
Atovaquone-proguanil chemoprophylaxis for the malaria areas, with primaquine terminal prophylaxis for 14 days after leaving them because of prolonged P. vivax exposure
Repellent, permethrin-treated clothing, bed nets and screened quarters against mosquitoes, fleas, lice and mites; food and water precautions with standby azithromycin for severe travelers' diarrhea
consultant_note.communication: Discussed with Dr. Delacroix-Boateng, who saw him the same day. The diagnosis and plan were explained to Mr. Le Moyne d'Iberville, who agreed and took the first chloroquine dose in clinic
